A.explanation: This is the average power over 5 s, $50/5 = 10 \text{ W}$, not the maximum instantaneous power.

B.explanation: This is close to the average slope between 2 s and 5 s, about $40/3 \text{ W}$, not the steepest instantaneous slope.

C.explanation: The steepest gradient is between 2 s and 3 s, about $30 \text{ J}$ in $1 \text{ s}$, giving $30 \text{ W}$.

D.explanation: This confuses the total energy $50 \text{ J}$ with power, which is rate of energy transfer in $\text{W}$.

hints: Notice the y-axis is total energy in $\text{J}$ and the x-axis is time in $\text{s}$, so instantaneous power is the gradient $P = \Delta E / \Delta t$.
Look for where the energy-time curve is steepest - the flat part near 2 s has zero power and the curve after 3 s is much less steep.
Measure $\Delta E$ over the straight steep section from $t = 2 \text{ s}$ to $t = 3 \text{ s}$ and divide by $\Delta t = 1 \text{ s}$.
walkthrough: Instantaneous electrical power is the rate of generation of energy, $P = dE/dt$, which is the gradient of the energy-time graph.
Scan the graph for maximum gradient: 0 to 1 s is moderately steep, 1 to 2 s is flat with $P \approx 0$, 2 to 3 s is very steep and straight, after 3 s the slope becomes small again.
Read values on the steep straight section: at $t = 2 \text{ s}$, $E = 10 \text{ J}$ and at $t = 3 \text{ s}$, $E = 40 \text{ J}$.
Calculate the gradient: $P_{max} = \Delta E / \Delta t = (40 - 10) \text{ J} / (3 - 2) \text{ s} = 30 \text{ J} / 1 \text{ s} = 30 \text{ W}$.
Check units: $\text{J s}^{-1} = \text{W}$, and this exceeds the 5 s average of $10 \text{ W}$, as expected for a peak. This is option C.
